options: The design of shops and offices
The way choices are presented to people
The law on consumer rights
The range of goods a firm makes
questions.why: How options are laid out affects what people pick.

questions.q: A yoghurt is labelled "95% fat free" and not "5% fat". What is this an example of?
options: Framing
Mandated choice
Anchoring
Restricted choice
questions.why: The facts are the same, but the wording makes them sound better.

questions.q: Which of these is a nudge?
options: A ban on smoking in cars with children
A tax on sugary drinks
Putting healthy food at eye level in a canteen
A minimum price for alcohol
questions.why: A nudge changes how a choice is presented without banning anything or significantly changing incentives.

questions.q: Match each type of choice to its meaning.
pairs: What happens if you do nothing
questions.why: Defaults rely on inertia, restrictions limit options, and mandates force a decision.

questions.q: UK automatic enrolment into workplace pensions is an example of a default choice.
questions.why: Eligible workers are put in unless they opt out, so doing nothing means saving.

questions.q: Why do default choices tend to have such a big effect?
options: They raise people's incomes
Many people stick with whatever happens if they do nothing
They make the alternative illegal
They are always the cheapest option
questions.why: Inertia and bounded self-control mean many people never change the default.

questions.q: Which is a valid criticism of government nudges?
options: They are always more expensive than taxes
They remove all freedom of choice
They rest on a value judgement about what is best for people
They only work on firms
questions.why: Someone has to decide what is "better", which is a normative question. Nudges are usually cheap and keep freedom of choice.

questions.q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using a nudge rather than a ban to reduce unhealthy eating.

ideas.label: Advantage: keeps freedom of choice, or is cheap and easy to bring in
Disadvantage: the effect may be small, fade, or be ignored

questions.model: A nudge keeps freedom of choice and is usually cheap to bring in, unlike a ban. But its effect may be small, because people can ignore it and still eat unhealthy food, so it may not solve the problem.
questions.why: A good answer gives one point on each side.

tests.answer: People keep their freedom to choose, but the effect may be small as they can ignore it.
It is cheaper for the government.
